title: Base or head: choosing the lever for each side
outcomes: Names the base and the head of a chain in an unlabeled position and picks the lever that attacks the base rather than the head
Tells a position with a chain from one without, before choosing a lever
As the chain's owner, chooses the move that answers the other side's plan instead of pushing a lever at once

steps.text: In **Pawn chains: hit the base, not the head** you learned the words and the lever. Now choose in positions where nobody tells you the plan. Rule of thumb: each side usually plays against the base of the other side's chain, and the owner often has to deal with the other side's plan before pushing a lever of their own. Start by naming the base: the pawn that defends another and that no pawn defends.

steps.caption: Black to move in a Caro-Kann Advance. White's chain is d4 and e5; d4 is the base, e5 the head.

line.say: c5 attacks the base d4, the pawn that no pawn defends.
White supports the base with c3.
A second attacker joins on d4.

steps.text: **Rule of thumb, with conditions.** A lever at the base works only when there is a chain to hit; without one it hits nothing. It also needs preparation: pieces that attack the same pawn. The chain's owner does not wait to be hit; the owner often needs the move that answers the other side's plan (a solid move may be better than a lever). The three positions below differ by one feature, and the lever is the same each time.

steps.title: Same lever, the chain changes
steps.prompt: Predict for each position whether ...c5 is a reasonable move. In the second a White bishop stands on another square; in the third a Black bishop does.
Before you push a lever at a chain, write its name: base or head. Then write whether your pieces are ready. Which do you expect to get wrong more often?
